title: Echinacea
subtitle: The purple coneflower: short-course tinctures and infusions for colds
excerpt: Echinacea is the purple coneflower, grown across North America and widely cultivated in kitchen gardens for its dramatic flowers and its long Eclectic-American use as a short-course herb at the start of a cold. The root and aerial parts are prepared as a tincture taken for 7 to 10 days at onset. A bottle of tincture keeps two years in a dark cupboard.
sourceNotes: King's American Dispensatory (Felter & Lloyd, 1898), Echinacea entry. Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), echinacea entry, Botanical.com. EMA HMPC monograph on Echinacea purpurea (L.) Moench, herba, EMA/HMPC/104918/2006 Rev. 2, open access. Cochrane review: Karsch-Völk M et al., Echinacea for preventing and treating the common cold (2015), Cochrane Database Systematic Reviews.

glossaryTerms.definition: A herb or preparation traditionally understood to modulate the body's immune response, historically used at the onset of infection rather than as a long-term tonic.

content.text: Echinacea in the home medicine cupboard, an herbal extract of the root and aerial parts taken for 7 to 10 days at the first sign of a cold. The central short-course herb of the North American Eclectic tradition, carried into modern western herbal practice for its traditional use at the start of an upper respiratory infection. A 100 ml bottle of herbal extract, prepared at 1:5, holds about 20 doses. it keeps two years in a dark cupboard.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor before use. Full precautions are in the 'When not to use' section.

content.text: Echinacea purpurea (L.) Moench, family Asteraceae. A robust perennial, 60 to 120 cm, with large purple (or sometimes white) daisy-like flowers with a distinctive spiny central cone, the origin of the name coneflower. Native to eastern North America from Kansas to Ohio, growing in prairies and open woodland. widely naturalised and cultivated in European gardens. The aerial parts (flowers, stems, leaves) and root are both used medicinally. E. angustifolia and E. pallida are also used. most modern European products are based on E. purpurea.

The root and aerial parts carry alkamides, caffeic acid compounds, polysaccharides, and glycoproteins. These groups are the focus of most modern plant compound research. Echinacea is used in western herbal practice at the onset of a cold as an
: taken to support the body's own immune response. Some clinical trials found it reduced cold incidence and duration, though results varied by product.

American herbalists of the late 1800s used echinacea for infected wounds and fatigue. European interest grew in the 20th century. Current guidance supports its use for respiratory illness at the start of a cold and for minor wounds.

Herbal extract of fresh herb (1:2 in 40 to 60% spirit): prepared from fresh aerial parts at flowering. The fresh-plant herbal extract is considered by many herbalists to be more potent than the dried-herb preparation, and is the form most traditional to the Eclectic-American use. Dose: 3 to 5 ml in a little water, up to four times a day, for 7 to 10 days at onset.

Infusion (aerial parts, dried): 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried herb per 200 ml water, steep covered 10 minutes. Three cups a day for 7 to 10 days. The infusion is weaker than the herbal extract and best suited to those who avoid alcohol.

Asteraceae allergy: echinacea belongs to the daisy family. If you have a confirmed allergy to ragweed, chamomile, or daisy, avoid echinacea. You can patch-test under guidance. Cross-reactions are documented.

Autoimmune conditions: echinacea affects immune function. Do not use if you have a diagnosed autoimmune condition without specialist guidance. Do not take alongside drugs that suppress the immune system. These include ciclosporin or tacrolimus.

Course length: traditional use, Eclectic texts, and current herbal guidance all support short courses of 7 to 10 days at the onset of or during a cold. Long-term daily use is not the traditional pattern and is not supported by current herbal guidance.
